blocks.text: The opening identifies this instruction as King Lemuel’s and as teaching from his mother. This fits the book’s closing chapters, which preserve distinct voices associated with Agur, Lemuel, and Lemuel’s mother rather than presenting them all as Solomon’s words. A Greek form of Proverbs also places portions corresponding to these final collections in a different order and includes interpretive expansions, so readers should attend carefully to the voice and shape of the passage before treating every saying in the book’s final chapters as the same kind of instruction.

Verses 10–31 form an alphabetic acrostic: the poem is arranged around the successive letters of the alphabet. Its praise is not limited to appearance or domestic activity. The woman is portrayed as strong, economically active, skilled in labor and trade, attentive to her household, generous to the poor, wise in speech, and reverent toward the LORD. The poem’s final praise therefore gathers many dimensions of capable, fruitful living rather than isolating one trait as its whole point.

The mother’s warning to Lemuel joins clear judgment with responsibility for vulnerable people: a ruler must not let drink cause him to forget the law or distort justice, but must speak up and judge rightly for the poor and needy. This concern belongs alongside Proverbs’ broader attention to both diligence and material outcomes, and to wrongs such as dishonest scales, bribery, boundary theft, exploitative lending, oppression of the poor, and rulers who deny justice. The chapter therefore does not treat poverty as a simple measure of personal effort; it also names the duty to resist injustice.

sections.title: The Capable Woman and Public Justice
